Chapter 1: Leaving Home and Facing the Unknown
There comes a moment when everything you’ve known suddenly slips away, and the world you step into feels totally unfamiliar. Imagine being a teenager, saying goodbye to everything you love—your family, your friends, even the rhythm of your own city—because you have to. Not just for adventure, but out of necessity.
That’s exactly what happens to our young traveler. She’s shaped by the chaos and unrest back home, and as she boards a plane to Europe, her parents watch with a mix of hope and worry. Maybe distance will mean safety. Maybe it’ll open new doors. Still, the city she leaves behind tugs at her—a city filled with family gatherings, whispered warnings, and the constant background noise of political tension.
Touching down in Vienna, everything feels different. The air, the language, even the looks people give her. She’s placed in a boarding house run by nuns, where the rules are strict and the atmosphere is chilly. The other girls? Most of them come from privilege. They move through life so easily, laughing about parties and what to wear, complaining about things that—honestly—seem pretty trivial compared to what she’s used to. War, loss, and the fight for freedom are her normal, but here, they’re almost unthinkable.
At first, she tries to blend in—copying their style, joining in their laughter. But that gap, the one between her past and their present, just won’t close. Whenever she shares stories from home, the other girls listen, but you can feel their discomfort. Her experiences fascinate them, but they also don’t know what to say. Her resilience becomes something she’s proud of, and yet it’s exactly what makes her feel like she doesn’t belong.
School isn’t any easier. The classes are tough, and the teachers don’t really go out of their way to help. She finds herself missing the warmth of her family, the comfort of her mother’s hug, and the shared sense of purpose that came from surviving hard times together. Letters from home help—they’re like a lifeline—but each one reminds her of what she’s lost.
Loneliness starts to settle in, almost like a second skin. She tries to make friends, but cultural differences keep getting in the way. A few classmates are curious about her story, but most keep their distance, maybe a little wary of what they don’t get. So, she turns to art and music, pouring her feelings into sketches and finding comfort in melodies that sound like home.
Slowly, she learns to find her way around the city—little routines, favorite cafés, a park bench where she can just watch life go by. And she realizes something: exile isn’t just about missing a place. It’s about losing a part of who you are. Every day, she’s caught between who she was and who she’s trying to become. The longing for home never really leaves, but she starts to understand that surviving means adapting, even when it’s painful.
So, what’s the lesson in those early days? Starting over is tough. The ache of leaving never just fades away. But in those quiet moments—maybe sitting alone as the city lights come on—there’s a tiny spark of hope. Because with time, even in the most unlikely places, new roots can grow.
